faq.q: Who signs a certificate of trust in Colorado?
faq.a: Under Colo. Rev. Stat. ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ§15-5-1013(2), a certification of trust may be signed or otherwise authenticated by any trustee. The statute does not require all cotrustees to sign, though the certificate must identify the currently acting trustee and state the trustee's powers. The certificate must also state that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in a manner that would cause the representations to be incorrect.

faq.q: Can a bank in Colorado require the complete trust after receiving a certificate?
faq.a: Under Colo. Rev. Stat. The statute's reliance provisions protect persons who act in good faith on the basis of a conforming certificate The statute's reliance provisions protect persons who act in good faith on the basis of a conforming certificate and may enforce the transaction against trust property.

faq.q: Is a certificate of trust the same as a trust agreement in Colorado?
faq.a: No. A certification of trust under Colo. Rev. Stat. ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ§15-5-1013 is a short declaration summarizing the required contents, while the trust agreement is the full instrument containing the dispositive and distribution terms. The statute expressly provides that a certification need not contain the dispositive terms of a trust. A certificate that omits any required content does not conform to the statute.

blocks.common_mistakes: A certification that omits the statement that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in any manner that would make the representations incorrect falls short of ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ§15-5-1013(3)'s required contents. So does a certificate that leaves out the revocability statement and the identity of the person holding the power to revoke, because a title company handling a sale cannot confirm who must sign a deed without it. A certificate describing trustee powers that do not match the pending transaction, or signed by fewer than all cotrustees when the statute requires it, also fails the statute. Omitting the name in which title to trust property may be taken is another common error.
blocks.state_notes: Colorado's certification of trust statute, Colo. Rev. Stat. ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ§15-5-1013, is part of the Colorado Uniform Trust Code enacted by SB 18-180, effective January 1, 2019. Colorado is one of the more recent UTC adopters, and its trust code incorporates modern provisions including trust decanting, nonjudicial settlement agreements, alternative dispute resolution, virtual representation, and directed trusts. Colorado has abolished the common law rule against perpetuities for trusts created after July 1, 2006, allowing perpetual dynasty trusts. Colorado has no state estate or inheritance tax and a flat, low income tax rate.
